A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same PyHealth 2.0 toolkit, and their text, tables, figures, and appendices support reliable comparison. v2 inserts a Benchmark Results appendix; v1 Appendices F–K are retained as G–L rather than removed.

before.justification: v1 reports original MIMIC-IV processing-time, memory, caching, and code-count comparisons, plus chest X-ray classification, conformal coverage, and interpretability results in Appendix E.

after.justification: v2 retains those experiments and adds laptop processing measurements and downstream modeling, interpretability, and uncertainty-quantification results in Appendix F.

M1.justification: The nine-module architecture, patient/event representation, task schemas, model interfaces, and three-stage Dask/Polars/LitData processing pipeline are retained. Appendix F adds evaluations of models and post-hoc methods without documenting a revision to the proposed toolkit procedure.

E1.justification: Appendix F adds actual evaluations on MIMIC-III mortality/readmission, eICU mortality/length-of-stay/readmission, Medical Transcriptions classification, TUAB abnormality detection, and TUEV event classification. These substantially extend evaluated populations and tasks beyond v1's MIMIC-IV processing and chest X-ray examples. The corresponding dataset catalogues already existed in v1.

E2.justification: The original Pandas, PyHealth 1.16, and MEDS comparisons remain. Appendix F adds quantitative comparisons among EHR models, CNN/ResNet-18/ViT-B/32, text-embedding variants, and BIOT/ContraWR/SPaRCNet/TFM-Tokenizer, together with attribution and conformal-prediction comparator sets. These are evaluated comparisons, not merely added citations or catalogue entries.

E3.justification: New modeling experiments use a stated 20-epoch AdamW protocol with learning rate 0.0001, default hyperparameters, and no tuning or pretraining. They introduce task-specific predictive and faithfulness metrics and a TUEV conformal evaluation at alpha = 0.1. Processing tests additionally cover two laptops at four and eight workers; existing workstation settings are retained.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained X-ray error case, v2 adds quantitative attribution-faithfulness analysis on a mortality Transformer (Table 21) and prediction-set reliability comparisons involving vanilla, KDE-adjusted, KMeans-adjusted, and neighborhood conformal methods (Table 22). Actual laptop tests also examine the previously asserted resource-constrained feasibility.

E5.justification: v2 Table 22 introduces mean and standard deviation over random sample splits for empirical coverage and prediction-set size. v1 reports point estimates without this variability reporting. The split count and seeds remain unspecified, and most other results still lack uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: Existing workstation processing values remain unchanged. Table 3 adds, for example, MacBook results of 1,357 seconds and 7.43 GB at eight workers, while Tables 8–22 add extensive predictive and diagnostic results. Table 2 changes PyHealth 2.0 task code counts from 7/7/7 to 34/18/23 and PyHealth 1.16 from 24/7/7 to 27/14/16, altering rankings. Added hardware/model results are not same-setting performance gains.

T1.justification: Neither version develops new theorems or proofs, and the mathematical descriptions of existing components and conformal guarantees are retained. Added evaluation metrics and the TUEV miscoverage setting do not introduce new formal definitions or derivations.

C1.justification: The three headline contributions—comprehensive functionality, computational accessibility, and community-supported reproducibility—and the abstract's seven-line, 39-fold speed, and 20-fold memory claims remain. Explicitly naming text and five-plus uncertainty methods summarizes capabilities already documented in v1; the new experiments chiefly support retained contributions.

C2.justification: v2 substantially broadens interpretation and applicability qualifications: it attributes laptop advantages to storage, memory bandwidth, and single-core throughput; adds hardware/OS sensitivity, absent governance/de-identification tooling, and uneven modality maturity as limitations; and explains the code-count tradeoff through task identifiers and object-oriented design. Existing interpretability, distribution-shift, and multimodal limitations remain.

D1.justification: v2 adds an explicit code-archive link, a project-site pointer, laptop/storage specifications, and training settings for the new benchmarks. It removes the standalone Software and Data paragraph and PyHealth 2.0 pip-install instructions. The extensive existing implementation appendix is retained; detailed splits, sample counts, and repetition counts for the new benchmarks remain largely unspecified.

R1.justification: CovariateLabel's attribution changes from Fannjiang et al. (2022) to Tibshirani et al. (2019) and Laghuvarapu et al. (2023), with corresponding bibliography changes. The PyHealth research-initiative newsletter citation is removed. Positioning relative to MEDS, MONAI, Zensols, and existing benchmarks is otherwise retained.

P1.justification: v2 adds a benchmark appendix, hardware discussion, and an explicit limitations paragraph, with localized abstract and wording edits. Later appendices are renumbered, the Software and Data heading disappears, and publication information changes. Most existing prose and the overall narrative structure remain intact.

P2.justification: Figure 3 is redrawn with logarithmic axes, laptop curves, and expanded hardware labels and caption. Appendix F adds a substantial set of organized benchmark tables; Table 3 gains laptop rows and Table 2 is relocated with revised explanatory formatting. Figures 5–6 receive redesigned panels while retaining their underlying examples and results.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses an important evidence gap: actual 16 GB laptop measurements substantiate accessibility previously inferred from workstation tests, and Appendix F evaluates advertised modeling and reliability capabilities that v1 largely catalogued. Revised code-count comparisons and explicit hardware and component-maturity limitations make the account more balanced. Missing benchmark splits, sample counts, and repetition details still limit reproducibility, but the direct feasibility evidence and broader empirical scrutiny substantially strengthen the paper.
